source: Worden, Heffernan, Heffernan, Sonkar (2026) FoundationalASSIST
finding: Four open LLMs asked to predict whether a student answers the next item correctly barely beat the always-say-correct baseline.
numbers: Eval set N about 27,700; baseline acc 51.3%, AUC 0.500. GPT-OSS-120B 56.2% / AUC 0.559; Llama-3.3-70B 52.3% / 0.512; Qwen3-Next-80B-Instruct 54.0% / 0.539; Qwen3-Next-80B-Thinking 55.8% / 0.555. Data: ASSISTments, 1.7M interactions, 5,000 students, 3,400 items.
quote: Every model barely achieves a trivial baseline on knowledge tracing
limits: Prompted open models only; no frontier closed models; math K-12 only.
agent_relevance: An LLM asked to guess what a learner will get right is near chance. Do not trust the model's gut estimate of another mind's skill without data.

source: Worden, Heffernan, Heffernan, Sonkar (2026) FoundationalASSIST (optimism bias)
finding: LLMs show strong optimistic bias: they predict 'correct' too often and miss struggling students.
numbers: Llama-3.3-70B: 85.4% right when the student was correct, only 12.6% right when the student was wrong.
limits: One model reported in the intro; same prompt for all.
agent_relevance: Any agent that models a user or sub-agent should check for a 'they probably succeed' bias and calibrate against base rates.

source: Worden, Heffernan, Heffernan, Sonkar (2026) FoundationalASSIST (answer prediction)
finding: Predicting the exact answer a student will give is also weak.
numbers: Exact-answer accuracy: GPT-OSS-120B 41.2%, Llama-3.3-70B 44.3%, Qwen3-80B-Instruct 35.5%, Qwen3-80B-Thinking 38.5%.
limits: Open-ended fill-in items are about 70% of interactions, so chance is near zero for them.
agent_relevance: Predicting a specific wrong answer is a probe of a misconception; models do it only partly.

source: Worden, Heffernan, Heffernan, Sonkar (2026) FoundationalASSIST (pedagogical grounding)
finding: LLMs judge relative item difficulty well but fall below chance on item discrimination and on rare distractors.
numbers: Difficulty comparison up to 68.6% overall and 80.0% when items differ a lot; discrimination below 50% for all models (best 46.9%, Qwen3 Thinking); most-chosen distractor 47.9% vs 35.8% random; rarely-chosen distractor about 15 points below chance.
quote: LLMs have learned to recognize some common misconceptions but cannot distinguish likely from unlikely distractors.
limits: Pairwise comparison format; math only.
agent_relevance: Models know what is hard but not what is diagnostic. A scaffold that picks the next probe question should not rely on the model's sense of informativeness.

source: Worden, Heffernan, Heffernan, Sonkar (2026) FoundationalASSIST (reasoning effect)
finding: Explicit thinking helped abstract judgment but hurt concrete prediction.
numbers: Qwen3-80B-Thinking best on discrimination (46.9%) but worst on distractor prediction (20.5%).
limits: Authors' explanation (overthinking) is a belief, not tested.
agent_relevance: Extra reasoning is not uniformly good for modelling a learner; test per sub-task.

source: Hooshyar et al. (2025) Problems with LLMs for learner modelling
finding: Deep knowledge tracing beat a Llama 3 8B LLM, zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned, on next-step correctness on ASSISTments.
numbers: AUC: DKT 0.83, Llama zero-shot 0.69, fine-tuned 0.77. Accuracy: DKT 75%, zero-shot 64%, fine-tuned 72%. Zero-shot recall on incorrect answers only 20%. Fine-tuning took about 198 hours.
limits: One dataset (ASSISTments), one 8B model, split 80/10/10 by student.
agent_relevance: A small purpose-built tracker is stronger and cheaper than a general LLM as the state estimator.

source: Hooshyar et al. (2025) Problems with LLMs for learner modelling (temporal coherence)
finding: LLM mastery estimates move in unstable and sometimes wrong-direction ways across a sequence; DKT stays smooth and correct in direction.
numbers: Fine-tuned LLM has higher early-sequence errors; authors report fine-tuning lifts AUC about 8% over zero-shot but stays about 6% below DKT.
limits: Qualitative trajectories on a few learners; authors argue from this that LLMs will not match ITS effect sizes (a claim, not tested).
agent_relevance: Keep an explicit running state outside the model and update it by rule, rather than asking the model to re-estimate each turn.

source: Bhattacharyya et al. (2026) Faster, Cheaper, More Accurate (Eedi)
finding: Zero-shot LLMs predicting student answers lose to small knowledge tracing models and, for several, to a per-question average baseline.
numbers: Accuracy: LLM-KT (custom) 72.8%, SAKT 72.7%, DKT 71.8%, Gemini-2.5-flash-lite 66.5%, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 64.6%, GPT-4o-mini 58.6%, Llama-1B zero-shot 33.5%, Llama-1B LoRA 71.0%; dataset-bias baseline 66.5%. Macro F1: 0.674, 0.669, 0.650 vs GPT-4o-mini 0.579, Qwen 0.533, Gemini 0.527.
limits: Eedi maths data; vendor authors; small models; prompt had a 10-question history with text, construct and misconception.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning a small model on the task beat prompting a big one. Prompted guesses of a learner do not beat the simple item-difficulty prior.

source: Bhattacharyya et al. (2026) Faster, Cheaper, More Accurate (Eedi) (latency and cost)
finding: LLMs are orders of magnitude slower and costlier per student than KT models.
numbers: Latency per student: DKT/SAKT under 0.25 s; GPT-4o-mini 3.1 s; Gemini 128 s; Qwen2.5-7B 3,299 s; Llama-1B variants 1,598.8 s. Authors report KT is 600-12,000 times cheaper to deploy at scale; one LLM cost cited as 11,991 USD per year at 100,000 students.
limits: Hardware differs between runs; authors note this.
agent_relevance: State tracking by an LLM call each turn is expensive; use cheap rule-based state where possible.

source: Eedi blog (2026) We benchmarked LLMs against purpose-built models
finding: Industry write-up of the same benchmark, seen only as a search snippet.
numbers: Same figures as the paper: LLM-KT 72.8%, SAKT 72.7%, DKT 71.8%.
limits: Not opened; vendor source.
agent_relevance: Duplicate of the Eedi paper line; weight once.

source: Norris, Gal, Bulathwela (2025) Next Token Knowledge Tracing (NTKT)
finding: Fine-tuning a small LLM (LLaMA 3.2) to predict correctness tokens from a history written as text beats classic deep KT models by more than 10 AUC points.
numbers: Eedi data. LLaMA 3B: F1 85.22, Acc 78.87, AUC 90.32. Baselines AUC: DKT 72.37, AKT 72.23, AKT-text 73.23, DTransformer 75.60. A no-fine-tune LLaMA row: F1 82.11, Acc 77.23, AUC 89.10 (row labels in the text extraction are ambiguous). 5 runs.
limits: One dataset; baseline AUC about 72 is low versus other papers; table extraction messy, so check the no-FT row.
agent_relevance: Putting the student history in plain text with question text gives a strong tracker. Text is the right interface for an LLM.

source: Norris, Gal, Bulathwela (2025) Next Token Knowledge Tracing (NTKT) (ablation)
finding: Question text carries most of the gain.
numbers: LLaMA 3B on Eedi: ID-only F1 79.16 / Acc 69.22 / AUC 77.06; concept tags 83.22 / 76.77 / 84.59; full text 85.22 / 78.87 / 90.32.
limits: Same single dataset.
agent_relevance: The content of the item, not only an ID, is what lets an LLM model skill. Keep item text in any state record.

source: Lee et al. (2024) Language Model Can Do Knowledge Tracing (LKT)
finding: Encoder language models (BERT family) with question text match or beat DKT on a large dataset, but not on a small one.
numbers: XES3G5M-T (5.5M interactions): DeBERTa-v3 AUC 0.8513, ACC 0.8421; RoBERTa AUC 0.8508; DKT AUC 0.7852, ACC 0.8173; AKT AUC 0.8207. DBE-KT22 (167k interactions): AKT AUC 0.7984 beat the best LKT, RoBERTa 0.7643.
limits: Encoders, not generative LLMs; DKT number for XES3G5M-T copied from another paper; 5-fold CV.
agent_relevance: Text helps when data is large; with little data classic models win.

source: Lee et al. (2024) Language Model Can Do Knowledge Tracing (LKT) (cold start)
finding: Pre-trained on one dataset, LKT outperformed DKT on a new dataset with no extra training, and was better at small data sizes.
numbers: Figure-based result (no table values read): LKT pre-trained on DBE-KT22 beats DKT on XES3G5M-T zero-shot.
limits: Only two datasets, both maths.
agent_relevance: Language models transfer across item sets; ID-based trackers cannot. Useful for new problem types.

source: Li et al. (2024) Explainable Few-shot Knowledge Tracing
finding: GLM4 and GPT-4 with a few student records and a cognition-guided prompt match full-data deep KT models on two of three datasets and give written explanations.
numbers: Accuracy (few-shot LLM vs DKT): FrcSub GLM4 0.7939, GPT-4 0.7968 vs DKT 0.7481; MOOCRadar GLM4 0.8489, GPT-4 0.8246 vs DKT 0.8210; XES3G5M GLM4 0.8491, GPT-4 0.8176 vs DKT 0.8355 (AKT 0.8435). GLM3-6B much worse (0.54-0.66) and often broke the output format.
limits: Binary predictions so no AUC; best mode per model; baselines trained on full set; GPT-4 sometimes wrongly assumed a student got an item wrong.
agent_relevance: Few-shot prompting with explicit state-analysis steps can work for strong models only. Small models break format.

source: Li et al. (2024) Explainable Few-shot Knowledge Tracing (shots and text)
finding: More few-shot records help a lot, though too many cause confusion; item text helps, concept tags help little; random shots beat first-k shots on long histories.
limits: Exact point where extra shots hurt not read.
agent_relevance: Which history goes into context matters: pick relevant, not earliest, records. That is a retrieval rule for agent memory.

source: Li et al. (2025) CIKT: Collaborative and Iterative Knowledge Tracing
finding: An Analyst LLM writes a text profile of each student and a Predictor uses it; the loop is refined by feedback on prediction accuracy. It beats DKT-family models and raw GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1.
numbers: ASSIST2009 ACC: CIKT-Llama3.1-8B 0.775, CIKT-Qwen2.5-7B 0.777, best classic DIMKT 0.749, DKT 0.737, GPT-4o 0.732, DeepSeek-R1 0.669. F1: 0.827 and 0.820 vs GPT-4o 0.794 and R1 0.762. (Column mapping inferred from table order.)
limits: Binary metrics only, no AUC; sequences truncated by context; table read by position.
agent_relevance: This is a state-tracking loop inside an LLM: profile, predict, score, refine. Close to a scaffold pattern: a written learner model audited against outcomes.

source: Li et al. (2025) CIKT: Collaborative and Iterative Knowledge Tracing (ablations)
finding: Removing iteration, the profile, or the two-part cooperation each lowers results; performance levels off around 3 refinement rounds.
numbers: ASSIST2009 Llama: full ACC 0.775 vs 0.766 without iteration-and-cooperation, 0.772 without iteration, 0.755 without profile at inference. Rounds tested 0-3 on ASSIST2012.
limits: Gaps are about 0.01 to 0.02 with no significance test reported.
agent_relevance: A written profile helps a little, not hugely.

source: Scarlatos et al. (2025) Exploring Knowledge Tracing in Tutor-Student Dialogues using LLMs (LAK25)
finding: In open tutoring dialogue, GPT-4o labels knowledge components and correctness, and a fine-tuned LLM tracer (LLMKT) predicts next-turn correctness better than BKT, DKT, DKVMN, AKT, SAINT and simpleKT.
numbers: CoMTA (623 labeled turn pairs, 164 KCs) AUC: LLMKT 65.79, DKT-Sem 61.82, BKT 52.50, DKT 53.20, majority baseline 50.0. MathDial (21x more data) AUC: LLMKT 76.71, DKT-Sem 66.18, AKT 63.31. MathDial Acc: 68.41 vs 62.17.
limits: Labels come from GPT-4o with human checks; best AUC about 76 is far below standard KT (above 80), so dialogue tracing is hard.
agent_relevance: Closest to an agent loop: track what a partner understands from free-text turns. Classic trackers fail with little data; LLM tracers need little.

source: Scarlatos et al. (2025) Exploring Knowledge Tracing in Tutor-Student Dialogues using LLMs (LAK25) (annotation quality)
finding: Human experts rated GPT-4o's correctness labels very high and KC labels moderate-to-high; at least 58% of dialogue turns map to more than one KC.
numbers: Rater scores are in Table 4 (not transcribed); 58% multi-KC share is from the text.
limits: Inter-rater reliability was volatile per the paper.
agent_relevance: Skill labelling by LLM is usable but multi-skill turns break one-skill-per-step assumptions.

source: Lu and Wang (2024) Generative Students (L@S)
finding: GPT-4 given an explicit profile of mastered, confused and unknown knowledge components imitates real students' multiple-choice answers.
numbers: 45 generative students vs 100 real college students on 20 MCQs (heuristic evaluation). Per-question mean score Pearson r = 0.72 with real students; random-profile students r = -0.16. Cronbach alpha: generative 0.6176, real 0.559, random 0.042. Overlap with real students on hard questions: 3.
limits: One topic, one small item set; GPT-4 over-weights stated confusion and is too pessimistic on some items.
agent_relevance: A KC profile in the prompt, in the style of an overlay learner model, makes simulated answers track skill. The same format could describe what a sub-agent knows and does not.

source: Lu and Wang (2024) Generative Students (L@S) (behaviour by profile)
finding: Simulated students answer well when the correct answer is a mastered rule; they fail when the right answer is unknown and a confused rule is among the options.
numbers: Choosing the confused rule: 59.4%, 82.2% and 46.2% in the three scenario columns of Table 3 (column labels not recovered); 27.6% wrong when a confused rule was among options and the right answer was mastered.
limits: Authors note pessimistic over-generalisation of confusion.
agent_relevance: Profile-conditioned role play produces coherent but exaggerated error patterns.

source: Pardos and Bhandari (2023) Learning gain differences between ChatGPT and human tutor hints
finding: ChatGPT-written algebra hints in an adaptive tutor gave smaller learning gains than human-written hints, and 30% of hints were rejected for wrong answers or steps.
numbers: 77 Mechanical Turk adults, 2x2 design. Learning gain: Elementary human 24.63% vs ChatGPT 11.14%; Intermediate human 23.65% vs ChatGPT 1.7%. Human gains significant, ChatGPT gains not; difference p = 0.038 in both lessons. Intermediate pre-test imbalance (50.94% vs 80.05%, p = 0.0029).
limits: Early 2023 ChatGPT, small N, ceiling effects, worked-solution format confounded with generator.
agent_relevance: LLM-authored scaffolding needs a verifier; about one in three hints was wrong.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning (Sci Rep)
finding: A custom GPT-4-based physics tutor with pedagogy rules beat an in-class active-learning lesson in a crossover RCT at Harvard.
numbers: Median post-test 4.5 (AI, N=142) vs 3.5 (active, N=174); pre-test median 2.75 (N=316). Effect size 0.63 by linear regression, 0.73 to 1.3 SD by quantile regression (ceiling-corrected); p < 1e-8. Median time on task 49 min vs about 60 min in class.
limits: One course, one topic, short-term test; compared with a class, not a human tutor.
agent_relevance: The recipe (step by step, pre-written solutions, scaffold rules, no dumping answers) is a scaffold that worked. The model held correct solutions, so it did not need to solve and track.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Tutor CoPilot (RCT)
finding: LLM suggestions to human tutors, built from expert think-aloud reasoning, raised student mastery, mostly for weaker tutors.
numbers: RCT, over 700 tutors and 1,000+ students. Exit-ticket pass 62% control to 66% treatment (+4 points, p<.01); up to +9 points for lower-rated tutors; about 20 USD per tutor per year; 350,000+ messages show more probing questions and less generic praise. Participation points and survey outcomes: no significant effect.
limits: Proximal outcome (exit ticket), one provider, one district; effect shrinks as tutor quality rises.
agent_relevance: Human-in-loop with an LLM that models expert reasoning has an RCT result. Encoding an expert's decision rules works.

source: Corbett and Anderson (1994) Bayesian knowledge tracing, as cited by CIKT and Scarlatos et al.
finding: Modern LLM-KT papers use Bayesian Knowledge Tracing as the baseline; it keeps a binary mastery variable with learning and forgetting parameters. Seen only as cited.
numbers: In the dialogue paper, BKT AUC was 52.50 on CoMTA, near chance.
limits: Original paper not opened here; covered by other angles.
agent_relevance: BKT is the cheap rule-based state update an agent could run beside the model.

source: Synthesis across the lines above: where LLMs beat or lose to classic KT
finding: Pattern: prompting an LLM to guess learner success is near the prior; fine-tuning on text histories beats ID-based KT; hybrids with a written profile beat both.
numbers: Zero-shot AUC 0.512 to 0.69 (FoundationalASSIST, Hooshyar); fine-tuned LLM AUC 0.77 (Hooshyar) to 0.90 (NTKT); DKT 0.83 on one set and 0.72 on another, so the dataset changes the ranking.
limits: Different datasets, metrics and baselines; cross-paper comparison is rough.
agent_relevance: Rank claims by dataset. Use the LLM to read text and a tracker for the number.

source: Synthesis: methods from this subfield already used in LLM-agent loops
finding: In use: written learner profile refined by feedback (CIKT), KC-labelled turn tracing (LLMKT), KC mastery profile in the prompt (Generative Students), pedagogy-rule tutor with stored solutions (Kestin), expert-reasoning suggestions (Tutor CoPilot).
numbers: Gains: CIKT +0.01 to +0.04 ACC over classic; Tutor CoPilot +4 points; Kestin 0.73-1.3 SD.
limits: Only Kestin and Tutor CoPilot are randomized trials; the rest are offline prediction.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the schema: a per-subgoal known / unsure / unknown record, updated by rule and audited, with the model reading text but not guessing numbers.
